Messages.Author: legb...@my-deja.com
Messages.Body:
As i was re-posting the latest UK ratings one of the University buildings
was struck by lightning - propbably the one next door to where i work
[cries of: "serve you right for not posting earlier, you lazy old
bastard!" from the UK VTES community]. i know this because i heard the
flash earthing [loud electrical click], followed by a massive clap of
thunder, and car-alarms going off. About two minutes later the emergency
vehicles arrived so i hope no-one has been hurt - it isn't a fire alarm,
i'm sure of that. Anyway the interesting point is that despite being no
more than 50 yards from the point of impact, there WAS a noticeable delay
between the strike and the associated thunder - half a second, maybe. i
reckon sound travels a bit less than 1200 ft/sec, so i guess that means
that the sound you hear actually comes from above. But it looks to me
that the clouds are well over 1000 feet above, so it's not the sound of
two clouds clapping like i was taught by my thoroughly-mendacious
geography teachers. Any climatological gurus on the NG care to enlighten
my secondary-school level darkness about what, exactly, thunder IS?

Sent via Deja.com http://www.deja.com/
Share what you know. Learn what you don't.

Messages.Author: Richard Zopf
Messages.Body:
>Umm, we are seeing so many theories put forth here I am hesitant to
>enter the fray, but I think the insulation provided by your tires is
>worthless when you consider the voltages of lightning.

Ooh, ooh. Pseudo-chemistry (really materials science) stuff! I'm not quite
in my element, but...
The insulation value of rubber is ca. 500 Volts per mil (thousandth of an
inch), as compared to air at roughly 75 Volts per mil. You're right, in
that the distances involved as compared to the voltage of the bolt
(estimated in gigavolts, really big) make the insulation value of the
rubber negligible. The only thing the higher insulation value results in is
heat generated on the surface of the tire, as it resists the electricity
flowing through and around it. That's why the tires melt so often when a
car gets hit.

>It just arced
>across hundreds/thousands of feet of air- the 6 inches between your car
>and the ground don't matter much, tires or not.

Exactly. Although electricity will tend to go over the surface of the
rubber tires in its travel to reach ground. It will also arc from the metal
drivetrain to the ground. Rubber will also give the slight delay in
discharge of some residual electricity (whatever the car can store as a
capacitor) Thus the static discharge as you step out of the charged car
(time after the strike determines how strong this would be. You'd have to
be pretty quick to get enough of a jolt to knock you down... either that or
your car would have to be really good at holding a charge, which they
typically aren't)

Cars are safe because
>the electricity flows around the outside of the car (it being a nice
>conducting surface)

So long as you have a conductive exterior (and not polymer) or a metal frame
(like a Saturn; polymer body, steel frame)...

> rather than through it- so if you are inside the
>car, you won't get hurt. Not because the car is safe, but because the
>_inside_ of the car is safe.
>

This is true only as long as the exterior is more conductive than the
interior...

>I have no clue if the cars electircal systems would survive. I tend to
>doubt it, but can't make a useful comment.
>

I'm surprised we don't have an EE who plays Jyhad... This part is black
magic to me, too...

Half right. Lots of stuff in the car might have stopped working, but
in actuality you'd be perfectly safe. The electrical charge would pass
around the outside of the car, leaving you unharmed. It has something to
do with the charge being broken down into positive and negative ions, and
all of one sort being outside (positive, I believe), while the others migrate
inside. Short of being in an actual grounded structure, the inside of a car
is one of the best places to be when lightning strikes.
